```{python}
#| tags: [setup]
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath("."))
from _pcpkg import *  # noqa: F401,F403
import doe_report as D
import tables as T          # complex tables: merged cells, footnotes (T.<builder>(...).show())
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as sstat
import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

DOC = "PCR-005"
UO = "protein_a"
UO_TITLE = "Protein A Chromatography (Step 5)"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- identity, dates
uo = CFG.unit_op(UO)
P = {p.key: p for p in uo.parameters}
ver, eff_date = doc_version(DOC)
scale_l = f"{V['commercial_scale_l']:,}"
plan_appr = PLAN_APPROVAL["PCP-005"]
chron = csv("study_chronology.csv")
chron = chron[chron["step"] == UO].set_index("id")
def win(sid):
    return f"{chron.loc[sid, 'start']} to {chron.loc[sid, 'end']}"
first_start = chron["start"].min()
last_end = chron["end"].max()

def g(x):
    return f"{x:g}"
def rng(p):
    return f"{p.prange[0]:g}–{p.prange[1]:g}"
def nor(p):
    return f"{p.nor[0]:g}–{p.nor[1]:g}"
def met(b):
    return "met" if b else "not met"
def yn(b):
    return "Yes" if b else "No"
def f0(x):
    return f"{x:,.0f}"
def f2(x):
    return f"{x:.2f}"
def f3(x):
    return f"{x:.3f}"
def p3(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- design structure
n_scr = doe_runs(UO, "screening"); n_rsm = doe_runs(UO, "rsm")
cp_scr = doe_centre_points(UO, "screening"); cp_rsm = doe_centre_points(UO, "rsm")
n_fact = n_scr - cp_scr
n_axial = n_rsm - n_fact - cp_rsm
n_fac = len(D.rsm_factors(UO))
rp = report_params(UO)
n_par = len(rp)
n_multi = int((rp["Study"] == "multivariate").sum()); n_uni = n_par - n_multi
cls = rp["Class"].value_counts()
n_wc = int(cls.get("WC-CPP", 0)); n_cpp = int(cls.get("CPP", 0)); n_kpp = int(cls.get("KPP", 0)); n_gpp = int(cls.get("GPP", 0))
rt_set = P["bed_height"].setpoint / P["flow"].setpoint * 60
rt_hi = P["bed_height"].setpoint / P["flow"].prange[1] * 60
rt_lo = P["bed_height"].setpoint / P["flow"].prange[0] * 60
rt_short = P["bed_height"].prange[0] / P["flow"].setpoint * 60
mc_n = f"{V['n_monte_carlo']:,}"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- criteria
iac = D.iac_table(UO).set_index("response")
acc = {r: D.effective_acceptance(UO, r) for r in ["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "leached_protein_a_ppm", "lmw_cesds_pct"]}
crit_hcp = f0(acc["pool_hcp_ng_mg"][1]); crit_lpa = f0(acc["leached_protein_a_ppm"][1]); crit_frag = f2(acc["lmw_cesds_pct"][1])
ds_hcp = g(iac.loc["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "ds_high"]); ds_lpa = g(iac.loc["leached_protein_a_ppm", "ds_high"]); ds_frag = f2(iac.loc["lmw_cesds_pct", "ds_high"])
fold_hcp = g(iac.loc["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "downstream_fold"]); fold_lpa = g(iac.loc["leached_protein_a_ppm", "downstream_fold"])
fold_frag = g(iac.loc["lmw_cesds_pct", "downstream_fold"]); add_frag = g(iac.loc["lmw_cesds_pct", "downstream_added"])
any_tight = bool(iac["tightened"].astype(bool).any())
r1 = D.rev1_criteria(UO).set_index("response")
r1_hcp = f0(r1.loc["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "high"]); r1_margin = g(r1.loc["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "margin"])
agg_lim = D.iac_limit("bioreactor", "aggregates_hmw"); acid_lim = D.iac_limit("bioreactor", "acidic_variants")
agg_crit = f2(agg_lim[1]); acid_crit = f"{acid_lim[0]:g}–{acid_lim[1]:g}"
lof_alpha = THRESHOLDS["lof_alpha"]; max_gap = THRESHOLDS["max_r2_minus_pred_r2"]

# platform worst cases this step's criteria rely on (checked downstream)
ver_all = D.iac_verification()
rel = ver_all[(ver_all["cqa"].isin(["hcp", "leached_protein_a", "fragments_lmw"])) & (ver_all["step_key"] != UO)]
rel_chk = rel[rel["met"].notna()]
n_rel = len(rel); n_rel_chk = len(rel_chk); n_rel_conf = int(rel_chk["met"].astype(bool).sum())

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- scale-down model qualification (TOST)
sdm = csv("sdm_qualification.csv"); sdm = sdm[sdm["step"] == UO]
SDM_RESP = ["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "step_yield", "leached_protein_a_ppm", "plates_per_m", "asymmetry"]
SDM_LABEL = {"pool_hcp_ng_mg": "Pool HCP (ng/mg)", "step_yield": "Step yield (%)",
             "leached_protein_a_ppm": "Leached Protein A (ppm)", "plates_per_m": "Column efficiency (plates/m)",
             "asymmetry": "Peak asymmetry"}
SDM_ND = {"pool_hcp_ng_mg": 0, "step_yield": 2, "leached_protein_a_ppm": 2, "plates_per_m": 0, "asymmetry": 2}
def tost(r, studies):
    a = sdm.loc[(sdm["scale"] == "scale-down") & sdm["study"].isin(studies), r].values
    b = sdm.loc[sdm["scale"] == "manufacturing", r].values
    k = 100 if r == "step_yield" else 1
    a, b = a * k, b * k
    diff = a.mean() - b.mean()
    margin = (b.max() - b.min()) / 2
    dfp = len(a) + len(b) - 2
    sp = np.sqrt(((len(a) - 1) * a.var(ddof=1) + (len(b) - 1) * b.var(ddof=1)) / dfp)
    se = sp * np.sqrt(1 / len(a) + 1 / len(b))
    tq = sstat.t.ppf(0.95, dfp)
    lo, hi = diff - tq * se, diff + tq * se
    return dict(n_a=len(a), n_b=len(b), ma=a.mean(), mb=b.mean(), diff=diff, lo=lo, hi=hi, margin=margin,
                eq=bool(lo > -margin and hi < margin), half=tq * se, df=dfp,
                below=bool((a < b.mean()).all()), above=bool((a > b.mean()).all()))
sdm_studies = sorted(sdm.loc[sdm["scale"] == "scale-down", "study"].unique())
SDM0 = {r: tost(r, ["S-PA-SDM"]) for r in SDM_RESP}       # the planned set-point runs alone
SDM = {r: tost(r, sdm_studies) for r in SDM_RESP}          # all scale-down set-point runs
def _sdm_row(r, t):
    fm = lambda x: f"{x:,.{SDM_ND[r]}f}"
    return [SDM_LABEL[r], f"{t['n_a']} / {t['n_b']}", fm(t["ma"]), fm(t["mb"]), fm(t["diff"]),
            f"{fm(t['lo'])} to {fm(t['hi'])}", f"± {fm(t['margin'])}", yn(t["eq"])]
_cols = ["Output", "n (SD / M)", "Mean, SD", "Mean, M", "Difference", "90 % CI", "Margin", "Equivalent"]
sdm_df = pd.DataFrame([_sdm_row(r, SDM[r]) for r in SDM_RESP], columns=_cols)
sdm0_df = pd.DataFrame([_sdm_row(r, SDM0[r]) for r in SDM_RESP], columns=_cols)
sdm_n_eq = sum(SDM[r]["eq"] for r in SDM_RESP)
sdm0_n_eq = sum(SDM0[r]["eq"] for r in SDM_RESP)
sdm_eq_names = [SDM_LABEL[r].split(" (")[0].lower() for r in SDM_RESP if SDM[r]["eq"]]
lpa_ratio = SDM["leached_protein_a_ppm"]["mb"] / SDM["leached_protein_a_ppm"]["ma"]
sdm_df_p = SDM["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]["df"]
sdm0_df_p = SDM0["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]["df"]
n_sd_all = SDM["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]["n_a"]
hcp_q = SDM["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]["eq"]          # qualified for pool HCP
y_q = SDM["step_yield"]["eq"]
pl_q = SDM["plates_per_m"]["eq"]
# outputs whose planned three-run interval could not meet the margin even at zero difference
SDM_NAME = {"pool_hcp_ng_mg": "pool host cell protein", "step_yield": "step yield", "leached_protein_a_ppm": "leached Protein A",
            "plates_per_m": "column efficiency", "asymmetry": "peak asymmetry"}
def andjoin(xs):
    xs = list(xs)
    return xs[0] if len(xs) == 1 else ", ".join(xs[:-1]) + " and " + xs[-1]
sdm0_short = andjoin(SDM_NAME[r] for r in SDM_RESP if SDM0[r]["half"] >= SDM0[r]["margin"])
sdm_eq_txt = andjoin(SDM_NAME[r] for r in SDM_RESP if SDM[r]["eq"])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- model fits and adequacy
RESP = ["pool_hcp_ng_mg", "step_yield", "leached_protein_a_ppm", "lmw_cesds_pct"]
F = {r: D.fit(UO, "rsm", r) for r in RESP}
FS = {r: D.fit(UO, "screening", r) for r in D.responses(UO)}
def gap(r):
    return F[r]["R2"] - F[r]["predR2"]
ADEQ = {r: dict(sig=F[r]["p"] < lof_alpha, lof=F[r]["p_lof"] >= lof_alpha, pred=gap(r) <= max_gap) for r in RESP}
for r in RESP:
    ADEQ[r]["all"] = all(ADEQ[r].values())

# reduced step-yield model: the terms significant in both designs, kept hierarchical
dY = csv(f"doe_{UO}_rsm.csv")
red_terms = ["coded_load", "coded_flow", "coded_end_collect", "coded_load:coded_flow"]
mY = smf.ols("step_yield ~ " + " + ".join(red_terms), dY).fit()
hY = mY.get_influence().hat_matrix_diag
predY = 1 - np.sum((mY.resid / (1 - hY)) ** 2) / np.sum((dY["step_yield"] - dY["step_yield"].mean()) ** 2)
sseY = float(np.sum(mY.resid ** 2)); df_peY = F["step_yield"]["df_pe"]; ss_peY = F["step_yield"]["ss_pe"]
df_lofY = int(mY.df_resid) - df_peY
FlofY = ((sseY - ss_peY) / df_lofY) / (ss_peY / df_peY)
p_lofY = float(sstat.f.sf(FlofY, df_lofY, df_peY))
RED = dict(R2=mY.rsquared, adj=mY.rsquared_adj, pred=predY, p=mY.f_pvalue, p_lof=p_lofY, gap=mY.rsquared - predY,
           k=len(red_terms) + 1)
RED["all"] = bool(RED["p"] < lof_alpha and RED["p_lof"] >= lof_alpha and RED["gap"] <= max_gap)
same_verdict_adj = all(((F[r]["adjR2"] - F[r]["predR2"]) <= max_gap) == ADEQ[r]["pred"] for r in RESP) and \
    ((RED["adj"] - RED["pred"]) <= max_gap) == (RED["gap"] <= max_gap)

adeq_rows = []
for r in RESP:
    f = F[r]
    adeq_rows.append([D.RESP_LABEL[r], "full quadratic", f3(f["R2"]), f3(f["adjR2"]), f3(f["predR2"]), f3(gap(r)),
                      p3(f["p"]), p3(f["p_lof"]), yn(ADEQ[r]["all"])])
adeq_rows.insert(2, ["Step yield", f"reduced ({RED['k']} terms)", f3(RED["R2"]), f3(RED["adj"]), f3(RED["pred"]), f3(RED["gap"]),
                     p3(RED["p"]), p3(RED["p_lof"]), yn(RED["all"])])
adeq_df = pd.DataFrame(adeq_rows, columns=["Response", "Model", "R²", "Adj. R²", "Pred. R²", "R² − pred. R²",
                                           "Model p", "Lack of fit p", "Criteria 2–4 met"])

# residual checks (criterion 5): |residual| on predicted, and Cook's distance against 4/n
cook_lim = 4 / n_rsm
res_rows, RES = [], {}
for r in RESP:
    m = F[r]["model"]
    cd = m.get_influence().cooks_distance[0]
    gm = sm.OLS(np.abs(m.resid.values), sm.add_constant(m.fittedvalues.values)).fit()
    go = sm.OLS(m.resid.values, sm.add_constant(F[r]["df"]["run_order"].values.astype(float))).fit()
    RES[r] = dict(p_slope=gm.pvalues[1], p_order=go.pvalues[1], cmax=cd.max(), crun=int(F[r]["df"]["run"].values[cd.argmax()]),
                  n_over=int((cd > cook_lim).sum()), cd=cd)
    res_rows.append([D.RESP_LABEL[r], p3(gm.pvalues[1]), p3(go.pvalues[1]), f2(cd.max()), str(RES[r]["crun"]), str(RES[r]["n_over"])])
res_df = pd.DataFrame(res_rows, columns=["Response", "p, abs. residual on predicted", "p, residual on run order",
                                         "Largest Cook's distance", "Run", "Runs above 4/n"])
slope_ok = all(RES[r]["p_slope"] >= lof_alpha for r in RESP)
order_ok = all(RES[r]["p_order"] >= lof_alpha for r in RESP)
p_order_min = min(RES[r]["p_order"] for r in RESP)
n_over_min = min(RES[r]["n_over"] for r in RESP); n_over_max = max(RES[r]["n_over"] for r in RESP)
mean_lev = (F["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]["model"].df_model + 1) / n_rsm

# influence of single runs on the pool HCP conclusion (deletion of each run above 4/n)
fH = F["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]; XH = fH["model"].model.exog; yH = fH["df"]["pool_hcp_ng_mg"].values
nor_grid = list(itertools.product(*[[D.to_coded(UO, q, P[q].nor[0]), 0.0, D.to_coded(UO, q, P[q].nor[1])] for q in fH["factors"]]))
Gc = pd.DataFrame(nor_grid, columns=["coded_" + q for q in fH["factors"]])
XG = D._design(Gc, fH["factors"], True)[0].values
loo_max, loo_dA, loo_dB = [], [], []
pA, pB = fH["model"].params.iloc[1], fH["model"].params.iloc[2]
for i in np.where(RES["pool_hcp_ng_mg"]["cd"] > cook_lim)[0]:
    mi = sm.OLS(np.delete(yH, i), np.delete(XH, i, axis=0)).fit()
    loo_max.append(float((XG @ mi.params).max()))
    loo_dA.append(abs(mi.params[1] / pA - 1)); loo_dB.append(abs(mi.params[2] / pB - 1))
loo_lo, loo_hi = min(loo_max), max(loo_max)
loo_dmax = 100 * max(max(loo_dA), max(loo_dB))
loo_ok = loo_hi <= acc["pool_hcp_ng_mg"][1]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- centre points
cv_s = D.center_cv_df(UO, "screening").set_index("Response")
cv_r = D.center_cv_df(UO, "rsm").set_index("Response")
L = D.RESP_LABEL
cv_least = cv_r["%CV"].idxmax()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- effects and coefficients
def se_row(resp, term):
    e = D.screening_effects_df(UO, resp).set_index("Term")
    return e.loc[term]
def co_row(resp, term):
    c = D.rsm_coeff_df(UO, resp).set_index("Term")
    return c.loc[term]
scr_fit = D.fit_summary_df(UO, "screening").set_index("Response")
eH = {t: se_row("pool_hcp_ng_mg", t) for t in ["A", "B", "AB", "C", "D"]}
eY = {t: se_row("step_yield", t) for t in ["A", "B", "C", "D", "AC", "CD", "BD"]}
eL = D.screening_effects_df(UO, "leached_protein_a_ppm")
eL_nsig = int((eL["p-value"] < 0.05).sum())
cH = {t: co_row("pool_hcp_ng_mg", t) for t in ["A", "B", "C", "D", "AB", "AC", "AD", "BD", "B²"]}
cY = {t: co_row("step_yield", t) for t in ["A", "B", "C", "D", "AC"]}
cL = D.rsm_coeff_df(UO, "leached_protein_a_ppm")
cL_sig = cL[(cL["p-value"] < 0.05) & (cL["Term"] != "Intercept")]["Term"].tolist()
cF = D.rsm_coeff_df(UO, "lmw_cesds_pct").set_index("Term")
cF_sig = [t for t in cF.index if t != "Intercept" and cF.loc[t, "p-value"] < 0.05]
slope_hi = cH["B"]["Coef."] + cH["AB"]["Coef."]   # pH coefficient at high load (A = +1)
slope_lo = cH["B"]["Coef."] - cH["AB"]["Coef."]   # at low load (A = -1)
yred = mY.params
yC_hi = yred["coded_flow"] + yred["coded_load:coded_flow"]
yC_lo = yred["coded_flow"] - yred["coded_load:coded_flow"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- descriptive (no adequate model)
dS = csv(f"doe_{UO}_screening.csv")
lpa_all = pd.concat([dS["leached_protein_a_ppm"], dY["leached_protein_a_ppm"]])
lpa_min, lpa_max = lpa_all.min(), lpa_all.max()
lpa_scaled = lpa_max * lpa_ratio
lpa_ok = bool(lpa_scaled <= acc["leached_protein_a_ppm"][1])
fr = dY["lmw_cesds_pct"].dropna()
fr_n, fr_min, fr_max = len(fr), fr.min(), fr.max()
fr_ok = bool(fr_max <= acc["lmw_cesds_pct"][1])
frag_nom = V["fragments_nominal"]
sec_minus = (dY["lmw_sec_pct"] - dY["lmw_cesds_pct"]).dropna()
hcp_all_max = dY["pool_hcp_ng_mg"].max(); hcp_all_min = dY["pool_hcp_ng_mg"].min()
hcp_scr_max = dS["pool_hcp_ng_mg"].max()
y_min, y_max = 100 * dY["step_yield"].min(), 100 * dY["step_yield"].max()
n_hcp_over = int((dY["pool_hcp_ng_mg"] > acc["pool_hcp_ng_mg"][1]).sum() + (dS["pool_hcp_ng_mg"] > acc["pool_hcp_ng_mg"][1]).sum())

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- PAR, design space, capability
pt = D.par_table(UO); pt1 = D.par_table_rev1(UO)
def par(tab, cqa, param, col="PAR (NOR)"):
    t = tab[(tab["CQA"].str.startswith(cqa)) & (tab["Parameter"] == param)]
    return t[col].iloc[0]
NAMES = {q: P[q].name for q in D.rsm_factors(UO)}
hcp_par_nor = {q: par(pt, "Pool HCP", NAMES[q]) for q in NAMES}
hcp_par_sp = {q: par(pt, "Pool HCP", NAMES[q], "PAR (set-point)") for q in NAMES}
hcp_par_nor1 = {q: par(pt1, "Pool HCP", NAMES[q]) for q in NAMES}
lpa_par_nor1 = {q: par(pt1, "Leached", NAMES[q]) for q in NAMES}
n_hcp_narrow = sum(hcp_par_nor[q] != rng(P[q]) for q in NAMES)
narrow_q = [q for q in NAMES if hcp_par_nor[q] != rng(P[q])]
n_hcp_narrow1 = sum(hcp_par_nor1[q] != rng(P[q]) for q in NAMES)
gov_hcp = D.governing_factor(UO, "pool_hcp_ng_mg")
ds = D.design_space_grid(UO)
ds_frac = 100 * ds["fraction"]; ds_bind = L[ds["binding"]]
cr = T.criteria_results(UO)
cr_hcp_range = cr.body[0][3].text; cr_hcp_sp = cr.body[0][2].text
capd = cap_for(["hcp", "leached_protein_a", "fragments_lmw"]).set_index("CQA")
cpk_hcp = capd.iloc[0]["Cpk"]; cpk_lpa = capd.iloc[1]["Cpk"]; cpk_frag = capd.iloc[2]["Cpk"]
poos = D.p_oos().set_index("key")
n_oos = int(poos.loc[["hcp", "leached_protein_a", "fragments_lmw"], "n_oos"].sum())

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- hold study
hold = csv(f"hold_{UO}.csv")
def hv(temp, day, col):
    return hold[(hold["temperature"] == temp) & (hold["day"] == day)][col].iloc[0]
temps = list(hold["temperature"].unique())
t_cold, t_warm = temps[0], temps[1]
h_days = int(hold["day"].max())
h_hmw_max = hold["hmw_pct"].max(); h_acid_min = hold["acidic_pct"].min(); h_acid_max = hold["acidic_pct"].max()
h_ce_max = hold["lmw_cesds_pct"].max()
h_ok = bool(h_hmw_max <= agg_lim[1] and h_acid_min >= acid_lim[0] and h_acid_max <= acid_lim[1] and h_ce_max <= acc["lmw_cesds_pct"][1])
ce_days = sorted(hold.loc[hold["lmw_cesds_pct"].notna(), "day"].unique())

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- deviations, methods, references
devs = dev_facts(DOC)
n_dev = len(devs)
sops_pa = PROTEIN_A_SOP_REFS + [s for s in SOP_REFS if s[0] == "SOP-3015"]
amvs_pa = PROTEIN_A_AMV_REFS + [a for a in UFDF_AMV_REFS if a[0] == "AMV-3019"] + \
    [a for a in AMV_REFS if a[0] in ("AMV-3013", "AMV-3020")]

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- extra scalars
wr = [(p.prange[1] - p.prange[0]) / (p.nor[1] - p.nor[0]) for p in uo.parameters]
wr_min, wr_max = min(wr), max(wr)
h_daylist = ", ".join(str(int(x)) for x in sorted(hold["day"].unique())[:-1]) + " and " + str(int(hold["day"].max()))
_ov = pd.concat([dS, dY])
_ov = _ov[_ov["pool_hcp_ng_mg"] > acc["pool_hcp_ng_mg"][1]]
hcp_over_corner = bool(len(_ov) > 0 and (_ov["load"] == P["load"].prange[1]).all() and (_ov["elution_ph"] == P["elution_ph"].prange[0]).all())
n_terms = int(F["leached_protein_a_ppm"]["model"].df_model)
_capall = csv("capability.csv")
min_cpk_attr = _capall.loc[_capall["Cpk"].idxmin(), "cqa"]

# DEV-005-01: the run that used the low-pH elution buffer lot, and its effect on the model
import re as _re
_lots = csv("dev_lots.csv").astype(str)
```

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

This report presents the process characterization of the Protein A chromatography step (Step 5) of the A-Mab drug substance process. Protein A chromatography is the capture step of the purification train. It removes most of the host cell protein and DNA of the clarified harvest, and it adds one impurity of its own, Protein A ligand that leaches from the resin. The studies were run under the approved plan PCP-005 in a scale-down model of the commercial column, between `{python} first_start` and `{python} last_end`. The report follows the lifecycle approach to process validation [@fda2011], the enhanced approach of ICH Q8 and ICH Q11 [@ichq8; @ichq11] and the A-Mab case study [@amab2009]. This is Version `{python} ver` of the report. It re-analyses the same experiments as Version 1.0 against the criteria of PCMP-001 Version 2.0, issued under INV-001, and adds the fragment results by nrCE-SDS.

The step has `{python} n_par` process parameters. Of these, `{python} n_multi` were studied in a `{python} n_scr`-run screening design followed by a `{python} n_rsm`-run response-surface design, and `{python} n_uni` were studied one factor at a time. Protein load and elution buffer pH were classified as WC-CPPs, load flow rate and end of pool collect as KPPs, and operating temperature and bed height as GPPs. No parameter of the step was classified as a CPP.

- F1. With the `{python} dev_005_03_n_planned` set-point runs that PCP-005 planned, the confidence interval was wider than the equivalence margin for `{python} sdm0_short` even at zero difference, so equivalence could not be shown (DEV-005-03). A further `{python} dev_005_03_n_supplementary` set-point runs were made with the margins unchanged. Over all `{python} n_sd_all` scale-down runs the model is `{python} 'equivalent' if hcp_q else 'not equivalent'` to manufacturing scale for pool host cell protein and `{python} 'equivalent' if SDM['asymmetry']['eq'] else 'not equivalent'` for peak asymmetry. Leached Protein A is consistently lower in the scale-down model, which is expected from the longer hold of the manufacturing load before capture, giving its host cell proteases more time to cleave ligand. This study does not test that cause. The difference was accepted as a known scale effect, as PCP-005 §5.1 allows. Step yield and column efficiency were not shown equivalent. Their intervals exceed the margin on the low side by `{python} miss_tab('step_yield')` % and `{python} miss_tab('plates_per_m')` % of the margin (@sec-sdm).
- F2. Pool host cell protein rises with protein load and as elution buffer pH falls, and the two parameters interact. It falls as the end of pool collect is extended. The response-surface model for pool host cell protein meets criteria 2 to 4 of PCP-005 §7 and does not meet criterion 5 (finding F7, @sec-rsm).
- F3. Step yield rises with end of pool collect and falls with protein load and load flow rate, and flow rate costs yield mainly at high load. The full quadratic model fails the predictive criterion, and a reduced model with the terms significant in both designs meets criteria 2 to 4 of PCP-005 §7. Like every model of the study, it does not meet criterion 5 (@sec-rsm).
- F4. No adequate model results for leached Protein A, so its dependence on the parameters of the multivariate design is not resolved. Every run of both designs met its intermediate acceptance criterion of ≤ `{python} crit_lpa` ppm, with a highest result of `{python} f2(lpa_max)` ppm (@sec-rsm).
- F5. Fragments by nrCE-SDS fall slightly as elution buffer pH rises, and no adequate model results. All `{python} fr_n` response-surface pools met the criterion of ≤ `{python} crit_frag` %, with a highest result of `{python} f2(fr_max)` % (@sec-rsm).
- F6. Under the criteria of Version 2.0 the NOR-propagated PAR for pool host cell protein spans the whole range studied for protein load, load flow rate and end of pool collect. For elution buffer pH it is `{python} hcp_par_nor['elution_ph']`, against a range studied of `{python} rng(P['elution_ph'])`. Every output met its criterion across the NOR (@sec-par).
- F7. No residual trend against the predicted value or the run order was found for any response. Between `{python} n_over_min` and `{python} n_over_max` runs of each response-surface model exceed a Cook's distance of 4/n, so criterion 5 of PCP-005 §7 is not met. Deletion of any one of these runs does not change the conclusion for pool host cell protein (@sec-resid).
- F8. The Protein A eluate held at elution pH met its criteria for `{python} h_days` days at both `{python} t_cold` and `{python} t_warm`. Aggregate and acidic variants rose more at `{python} t_warm`. Fragments by nrCE-SDS rose at both temperatures, and the data do not show a temperature dependence (@sec-hold).
- F9. No difference from the set-point runs was detected at either end of the ranges of operating temperature and bed height, and every result met its criterion. With two runs at each end the intervals are wide (@sec-uni).
- F10. The effect of end of pool collect on pool host cell protein, and its interactions with protein load and elution buffer pH, have opposite signs in the screening and the response-surface designs. The difference is larger than the noise of the screening design, and its cause was not identified (@sec-rsm).

Under criterion 1 of PCP-005 §7 a model that fails qualification for an output is not used for that output. The qualification for pool host cell protein supports the PARs and the design space of that output. The scale-down model was not shown equivalent for step yield, so under the same criterion the step yield model is not used for any range or prediction. The KPP classes of load flow rate and end of pool collect rest on the direction of the yield effects, which both designs show, and not on the model (@sec-class). The main effects of protein load and elution buffer pH agree in direction with the platform history and the mechanism of the step. Load flow rate did not raise pool host cell protein as the mechanism predicts (@sec-mech).

At commercial scale the integrated model of the train gives a Cpk of `{python} f2(cpk_hcp)` for host cell protein, `{python} f2(cpk_frag)` for fragments and `{python} f0(cpk_lpa)` for leached Protein A in the drug substance, and `{python} 'no simulated batch' if n_oos == 0 else str(n_oos) + ' simulated batches'` of `{python} mc_n` fell outside these criteria. The Cpk for leached Protein A is not meaningful, because the simulated drug substance values lie below the limit of quantitation of the ELISA. Three deviations were recorded (DEV-005-01, DEV-005-02 and DEV-005-03). All three were investigated. The affected data were retained, and for DEV-005-03 supplementary runs were made. The results roll up into the Process Characterization Master Report PCMR-001.

# Introduction

## Product and unit operation

A-Mab is a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody whose primary mechanism of action is antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. It is developed by `{python} COMPANY` and is being transferred from development at the sending site to commercial drug substance manufacture at `{python} scale_l` L scale at the receiving site, under the Process Transfer Plan PTP-001. The drug substance is purified by the platform train of Protein A capture, low-pH viral inactivation, cation exchange, anion exchange, small virus retentive filtration and UF/DF.

Protein A chromatography is the first chromatographic step of the purification train. It is operated in bind and elute mode. The resin binds the antibody from the clarified harvest at neutral pH, while host cell protein, DNA and most other components of the feed are removed in the load flow-through and the wash. A low-pH buffer elutes the antibody into a small volume, and the eluate passes to low-pH viral inactivation (Step 6) without neutralization. The step is the principal point of clearance for host cell protein and DNA, and it partly clears fragments. It introduces one attribute of the CQA register, leached Protein A. Although Protein A chromatography removes some virus, no viral clearance claim is made for this step [@amab2009]. The modular claim rests on low-pH inactivation, anion exchange and virus filtration, and it is consolidated in PCMR-001.

## Objectives

The objectives of the characterization were the following, as PCP-005 §2 states them.

1. To qualify the scale-down model for the outputs of the step at set-point.
2. To identify which of the `{python} n_multi` parameters of the multivariate design, and which of their two-factor interactions, affect pool host cell protein, step yield and leached Protein A.
3. To fit response-surface models for pool host cell protein, step yield, leached Protein A and fragments by nrCE-SDS, and to judge their adequacy for prediction.
4. To determine the PAR of each multivariate parameter for each attribute with a criterion at the step.
5. To establish the effect of operating temperature and bed height over their ranges, one factor at a time.
6. To establish how long, and at which temperature, the Protein A eluate may be held at elution pH before viral inactivation.
7. To provide the data for the classification of every parameter of the step under SOP-4001, and to support the Stage 2 ranges and the control strategy.

## Regulatory and scientific basis

The study is part of Stage 1 (process design) of the lifecycle approach to process validation [@fda2011]. It follows the enhanced approach of ICH Q8(R2) and ICH Q11 [@ichq8; @ichq11], in which prior knowledge and risk assessment identify the parameters that may affect quality, and designed experiments then measure and bound those effects. Criticality is treated as a continuum, as ICH Q8(R2) describes it, and risk is managed under ICH Q9 [@ichq9]. The classification of parameters follows the decision logic of the A-Mab case study [@amab2009], as PCMP-001 §7.7 applies it. The documents this report depends on and feeds are listed below.

## Changes in this revision

Version 1.0 of this report was approved on `{python} rev1_date(DOC)`. Version `{python} ver` takes effect on `{python} eff_date` and is issued under `{python} INV['id']`. QA opened the investigation on `{python} INV['opened']` after its review of PCMR-001 Version 1.0 for BLA readiness, and closed it on `{python} INV['closed']` with the classification `{python} INV['classification']`. The investigation found that the criteria used to judge each step in the PAR analysis were not in any approved protocol and had been set after the data were seen (INV-001 finding 1). For this step, Version 1.0 judged pool host cell protein against ≤ `{python} r1_hcp` ng/mg. That limit was the drug substance criterion carried back through the nominal downstream clearance of this campaign and divided by a margin of `{python} r1_margin` (INV-001 finding 2). Leached Protein A was judged against the drug substance criterion, and fragments were not reported. @tbl-criteria-change sets the Version 1.0 limits beside the Version 2.0 criteria.

```{python}
#| output: asis
T.criteria_change(["protein_a"]).show()
```

The Version 2.0 criteria are intermediate acceptance criteria derived a priori by PCMP-001 §7.3. The criterion for pool host cell protein, ≤ `{python} crit_hcp` ng/mg, is wider than the Version 1.0 limit. The Version 1.0 limit was never approved and appears in no approved plan, and it is replaced by a criterion derived without data from the studies it judges. The rule that data may tighten a criterion and never loosen it applies to the Version 2.0 criteria from this revision on.

The experiments, the data and the fitted models are those of Version 1.0. What moved is the following.

1. The NOR-propagated PAR for pool host cell protein. Under the Version 1.0 limit it was `{python} hcp_par_nor1['load']` g/L resin for protein load, which ends inside the NOR of `{python} nor(P['load'])` g/L resin and made the upper end of the NOR appear unsupported. Under Version 2.0 it is `{python} hcp_par_nor['load']` g/L resin. For elution buffer pH it moved from `{python} hcp_par_nor1['elution_ph']` to `{python} hcp_par_nor['elution_ph']`, for load flow rate from `{python} hcp_par_nor1['flow']` to `{python} hcp_par_nor['flow']` cm/hr, and for end of pool collect from `{python} hcp_par_nor1['end_collect']` to `{python} hcp_par_nor['end_collect']` CV.
2. The NOR-propagated PAR of elution buffer pH for leached Protein A. Under the drug substance criterion of ≤ `{python} ds_lpa` ppm it was `{python} lpa_par_nor1['elution_ph']`. Leached Protein A is now judged against its intermediate acceptance criterion and reported descriptively, because no adequate model results for it (@sec-rsm).
3. Fragments by nrCE-SDS are reported for the first time. The retained response-surface pools and the hold samples of days `{python} ' and '.join(str(int(x)) for x in ce_days)` were tested in study S-PA-RET under AMD-001 (@tbl-methods-by-study). The SEC fragment results of both designs are kept in the record and are not used for any decision (INV-001 finding 6).
4. Each response-surface model is judged against the model adequacy criteria of PCP-005 §7, which Version 1.0 left to the analysis. The full quadratic model for step yield was replaced by a reduced model, and leached Protein A and fragments are reported descriptively (@sec-rsm).
5. The scale-down model qualification is reported against the equivalence test of PCP-005 §5.1. The planned set-point runs could not demonstrate equivalence whatever the means were, and `{python} dev_005_03_n_supplementary` supplementary set-point runs (study S-PA-SDM2) were made under DEV-005-03, with the margins unchanged (@sec-sdm).
6. The execution window of every study is recorded (@tbl-chronology, INV-001 finding 5).

The parameter effects and their directions are those of Version 1.0. Their discussion is extended in this revision (@sec-rsm). Acidic variants are not an output of this step, so the two-sided capability assessment of INV-001 finding 4 does not apply here.

# Prior knowledge and quality risk basis

## Platform and prior-product knowledge

The same capture step has been used to purify the platform antibodies X-Mab, Y-Mab and Z-Mab, and A-Mab through clinical manufacture. Their history establishes the mechanism of the step and the direction of its main effects.

Staphylococcal Protein A, immobilized on the resin, binds the Fc region of the antibody at the interface between the second and third constant domains of the heavy chain. When the pH is lowered, histidine residues at this interface become protonated, the interaction weakens, and the antibody is released. The expectations for each output follow from this mechanism.

Host cell protein reaches the eluate by two routes. Some binds weakly to the resin backbone or the ligand and is released when the pH drops, and some is associated with the antibody and is carried through as a complex. The host cell protein associated with the bound antibody is carried on the bed with it, so its amount rises with the mass of antibody loaded. A lower elution pH releases more of the weakly bound host cell protein with the product. Pool host cell protein was therefore expected to rise with protein load and as elution buffer pH falls. At high load more host cell protein is held weakly on the bed, so a low elution pH has more to release. An interaction between the two parameters was expected for this reason.

Step yield is lost when antibody breaks through during the load or remains on the column at the end of collection. Binding is limited by diffusion into the pores of the bead. For this reason breakthrough rises as the load approaches the dynamic binding capacity and as the residence time falls. A higher load flow rate shortens the residence time and lowers the dynamic binding capacity, and this costs yield only when the bed is close to capacity. Yield was therefore expected to fall with flow rate mainly at high load, and to rise as the end of pool collect is extended into the tail of the elution peak.

Leached Protein A comes from hydrolysis of the coupling chemistry and from cleavage of exposed ligand by host cell proteases in the load, and the leached fragments elute with the antibody because they still bind Fc. Leaching is highest on new resin. More protease activity in the load, for example after a longer hold of the clarified harvest before capture, is expected to cleave more ligand. Neither of these is a setting of the run, so within the ranges of one run leached Protein A was expected to be flat.

A fragment is captured only if it still carries Fc. Fab fragments flow through with the load, and the pool carries less fragment than the feed. A lower elution pH may add a little acid-catalysed hinge hydrolysis during elution. The pool also still carries host cell protein, part of which elutes in the low molecular weight window of SEC and is read as fragment. SEC therefore overstates fragments in this matrix, and nrCE-SDS does not (INV-001 finding 6). DNA is polyanionic and does not bind Protein A. Its clearance is large and was not expected to depend on the operating parameters within their ranges.

Protein A, when operated under platform conditions, does not separate glycan variants or charge variants, because it binds the Fc region independently of both [@amab2009]. Nor does it separate aggregate from monomer, since both carry Fc. In the Protein A characterization of the case study no process parameter had a significant effect on aggregate [@amab2009]. Aggregate formation at low pH over the inactivation hold is characterized in PCR-006. For these reasons glycan variants, charge variants and aggregate were not responses of the designs.

## Quality attributes in scope

Leached Protein A is the only attribute of the CQA register that this step introduces. The step is also the principal point of clearance for host cell protein and DNA, and it partly clears fragments. @tbl-cqa lists the attributes in scope with their drug substance criteria and the criticality level the register assigns. The register treats criticality as a continuum, as the A-Mab case study does [@amab2009]. Each attribute is a CQA with a level from very low (VL) to very high (VH), assigned with Tool #1, whose score is the product of impact and uncertainty.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(cqas_by_keys(["leached_protein_a", "hcp", "fragments_lmw", "residual_dna", "aggregates_hmw"]))
print()
print(": Quality attributes in scope of this report, with the drug substance criterion and criticality. {#tbl-cqa}")
```

The drug substance criteria do not apply to the Protein A pool directly. Cation exchange and anion exchange remove host cell protein, leached Protein A and fragments after this step, and judging the pool against the drug substance limit would fail every acceptable run. Each output of the step with a downstream dependence is therefore judged against an intermediate acceptance criterion (@sec-par). Residual DNA and aggregate were measured for information. Step yield is a performance attribute without an acceptance criterion, and it is used for the classification of parameters that act on process performance.

## Risk-based prioritization and parameter selection

RA-001 assessed every parameter of the step before characterization began. Each parameter was ranked on its potential impact on the CQAs and on process performance, and on its potential to interact with other parameters. RA-001 gives the scores and the rationale.

Protein load, elution buffer pH, load flow rate and end of pool collect were assigned to multivariate study. Each carries an effect expected from the mechanism, and the interactions of protein load with elution buffer pH and with load flow rate can only be estimated in a design that varies the parameters together. Operating temperature and bed height were assigned to univariate study. A higher temperature speeds the diffusion of the antibody into the pores, which raises the dynamic binding capacity, and it strengthens the hydrophobic contacts at the Fc–ligand interface, which makes elution slightly less complete. Over the range studied both effects were expected to be small against those of load and pH, and the resin manufacturer specifies binding capacity across that range. Bed height is held by the packing specification in manufacture, and at constant linear velocity it sets the residence time.

The ranges studied are between `{python} f'{wr_min:.1f}'` and `{python} f'{wr_max:.1f}'` times the width of the NOR. They show how the step behaves near and beyond the edges of routine operation, and they bound the knowledge space within which a PAR can be claimed.

# Materials and methods

## Scale-down model and its qualification {#sec-sdm}

The scale-down model is a laboratory column packed with the commercial Protein A resin and operated under SOP-2007 on the scaling principles of PCMP-001 §5. The bed height and the residence time of the commercial column were kept. Load, wash and elution volumes were normalized to column volumes, and buffers were made to the commercial recipes. Column efficiency was checked by plate count and peak asymmetry after packing, and both are compared with manufacturing scale below.

The model was qualified under SOP-1001 in study S-PA-SDM (`{python} win('S-PA-SDM')`), before the first run of the screening design, and in the supplementary study S-PA-SDM2 (`{python} sdm2_win`) made under DEV-005-03. Set-point runs of the scale-down model were compared with the `{python} SDM['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['n_b']` manufacturing-scale batches of A-Mab run at set-point. The outputs compared were pool host cell protein, step yield, leached Protein A, and column efficiency as plates per metre and peak asymmetry. Equivalence of the means was tested by two one-sided tests at α = 0.05, using a Student t interval with pooled variance. The equivalence margin for each output is half the range of the manufacturing-scale batches. The model is qualified for an output when the 90 % confidence interval of the difference in means lies within that margin.

With the `{python} dev_005_03_n_planned` runs of S-PA-SDM the half-width of the interval alone was larger than the margin for `{python} sdm0_short`, so equivalence could not be shown for them whatever the means were (DEV-005-03, @sec-dev). A further `{python} dev_005_03_n_supplementary` set-point runs were therefore made. The margins were not changed. @tbl-sdm gives the result over all `{python} n_sd_all` scale-down runs, with `{python} sdm_df_p` degrees of freedom.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(sdm_df.to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True, colalign=["left"] + ["right"] * 7))
print()
print(": Scale-down model qualification over all scale-down set-point runs (studies S-PA-SDM and S-PA-SDM2). SD, scale-down model. M, manufacturing scale. Difference and 90 % confidence interval (CI), scale-down minus manufacturing. Step yield in percentage points. {#tbl-sdm}")
```

The scale-down model met the equivalence criterion for `{python} sdm_n_eq` of the `{python} len(SDM_RESP)` outputs, `{python} sdm_eq_txt`.

For pool host cell protein the difference in means was `{python} f0(SDM['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['diff'])` ng/mg, and the interval of `{python} f0(SDM['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['lo'])` to `{python} f0(SDM['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['hi'])` ng/mg lies within the margin of ± `{python} f0(SDM['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['margin'])` ng/mg. The model is `{python} 'qualified' if hcp_q else 'not qualified'` for pool host cell protein.

For leached Protein A the scale-down mean was `{python} f2(SDM['leached_protein_a_ppm']['ma'])` ppm against `{python} f2(SDM['leached_protein_a_ppm']['mb'])` ppm at manufacturing scale, and the whole confidence interval lies below zero. `{python} 'Each scale-down run was below the manufacturing mean.' if SDM['leached_protein_a_ppm']['below'] else 'Most scale-down runs were below the manufacturing mean.'` PCP-005 §5.1 accepts a difference that is consistent in direction and explained by a known scale effect, provided this report carries it into the interpretation. The difference is consistent in direction, and a scale effect on leached Protein A is recorded for this step. Its expected cause is the longer hold of the clarified harvest before capture at manufacturing scale, which gives host cell proteases more time to cleave ligand from the resin. This study does not test that cause. The difference was accepted as a known scale effect. It is carried into the interpretation of leached Protein A in @sec-rsm, where the design results are scaled by the ratio of the manufacturing mean to the scale-down mean, `{python} f2(lpa_ratio)`.

For step yield the difference in means was `{python} f2(SDM['step_yield']['diff'])` percentage points. The interval of `{python} f2(SDM['step_yield']['lo'])` to `{python} f2(SDM['step_yield']['hi'])` points extends beyond the margin of ± `{python} f2(SDM['step_yield']['margin'])` on the low side, by `{python} miss_tab('step_yield')` % of the margin, so equivalence was not shown. No known scale effect applies to step yield. Under criterion 1 of PCP-005 §7 the step yield model is therefore not used for any range or prediction. The yield effects reported in @sec-rsm describe the scale-down model. Their direction, which both designs show, supports the KPP classes in @sec-class, and their size at manufacturing scale is not established.

For column efficiency the scale-down column averaged `{python} f0(SDM['plates_per_m']['ma'])` plates per metre against `{python} f0(SDM['plates_per_m']['mb'])` at manufacturing scale. The interval of `{python} f0(SDM['plates_per_m']['lo'])` to `{python} f0(SDM['plates_per_m']['hi'])` extends beyond the margin of ± `{python} f0(SDM['plates_per_m']['margin'])` on the low side, by `{python} miss_tab('plates_per_m')` % of the margin, so equivalence was not shown. Peak asymmetry was equivalent. Column efficiency is a check of the packing and not a response of the characterization, so no result of this report depends on it directly. A lower plate count would broaden the peaks of the laboratory column. Pool host cell protein, which depends on how sharply the product elutes, was nevertheless shown equivalent.

Fragments by nrCE-SDS were not part of the qualification, because the analytical method decision AMD-001 was taken after the model was qualified. The model is taken as representative for fragments on mechanism. Capture of Fc-bearing species and low-pH hinge hydrolysis do not depend on scale at equal bed height, residence time and elution pH.

## Operation

Each run followed SOP-2007 at laboratory scale. The column was equilibrated, loaded with clarified harvest to the target protein load, washed, and eluted with the elution buffer at the pH set by the design. The eluate was collected from the rise of the absorbance at 280 nm until the end of pool collect set by the design, in column volumes. The column was then stripped, cleaned and stored under SOP-2008. The pool was not neutralized, because the commercial eluate passes to low-pH viral inactivation at elution pH.

Each design was loaded from one pool of clarified harvest produced at set-point and held frozen in aliquots. A single feed keeps feed variation out of the estimated effects. The effect of feed quality on the step was therefore not estimated in these studies. The case study reports that Protein A capture is robust over a wide range of feed inputs [@amab2009], and the feed is characterized in PCR-003 and PCR-004. Runs were executed in random order within each design. The resin was used within the life-cycle limits of SOP-2008, and the life cycle of the resin is outside the scope of this report.

## Analytical methods

Each response was measured by a validated method under its own AMV. The controlled procedures and method validations used are listed below. The SOP and AMV numbers are placeholders.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(sop_table(sops=sops_pa, amvs=amvs_pa))
```

Pool host cell protein was measured by ELISA (AMV-3012) and is reported per mass of antibody in the pool, so that it does not depend on how far the pool is diluted by the end of pool collect. Step yield is the mass of antibody in the pool divided by the mass loaded, from the protein concentration by absorbance at 280 nm (AMV-3019) and the measured volumes. Leached Protein A was measured by ELISA (AMV-3016). Fragments were measured by nrCE-SDS (AMV-3020, under SOP-3015), as PCMP-001 §7.8 sets for every step. SEC (AMV-3011) remains the method for aggregate, where no co-elution of this kind applies. Acidic variants in the hold study were measured by icIEF (AMV-3013), and residual DNA by qPCR (AMV-3014). @tbl-methods-by-study shows which method measured fragments in which study of the step, and Appendix D summarizes the methods.

```{python}
#| output: asis
T.methods_by_study(["protein_a"]).show()
```

The screening design ran before AMD-001, and its pools were not retained. Its fragment results are by SEC only and are not used for any decision. The response-surface pools were retained frozen and were tested by nrCE-SDS in study S-PA-RET (`{python} win('S-PA-RET')`). On those pools SEC read fragments higher than nrCE-SDS by `{python} f2(sec_minus.min())` to `{python} f2(sec_minus.max())` percentage points (median `{python} f2(sec_minus.median())`), which is the bias that INV-001 finding 6 describes for a matrix that still carries host cell protein.

## Sampling plan

The load of each design was sampled once per feed aliquot thawed. The pool of every run was sampled once at the end of collection, after mixing, and its volume was recorded. Each pool sample was divided into aliquots for each method. One further aliquot of every response-surface pool was retained frozen under the sample management procedure of Analytical Development, and these are the samples tested by nrCE-SDS in study S-PA-RET. The screening design had `{python} cp_scr` centre points and the response-surface design `{python} cp_rsm`. Residual DNA was measured on the load and pool of the centre-point runs. The hold study was sampled as described in @sec-holddesign.

## Statistical methods

The designs were built and analysed under SOP-1002 with the common approach of PCMP-001 §6. Factors were coded from −1 to +1 over their range studied, with 0 at the centre. For each of the `{python} n_fac` design factors the centre of the range studied is the set-point, so the centre-point runs of both designs are set-point runs.

The screening data were fitted with a model of main effects and two-factor interactions. Effects are reported as the change in the response over the coded range of the factor, which is twice the coefficient. Significance was judged at α = 0.05. The screening model identifies effects. A two-level design cannot resolve curvature, so the screening model was not used to predict between its corners.

The response-surface data were fitted with a full quadratic model. This is the predictive model of the step, and every PAR and every prediction of a quality attribute in this report comes from it. Step yield is the exception, because its full quadratic model failed criterion 4 and was replaced by a reduced model (@sec-rsm). Coefficients are reported in coded units, so that each measures the change in the response over half the range studied. Effects quoted from them are twice the coefficient. Each model is reported with R², adjusted R² and predicted R² (from PRESS), the model F-test, and the test of lack of fit against pure error from the centre points. The adequacy criteria of PCP-005 §7 were applied as follows.

The numbers are those of PCP-005 §7, where criterion 1 is the qualification of the scale-down model (@sec-sdm).

2. Model significance. The model F-test is significant at α = `{python} g(lof_alpha)`.
3. Lack of fit. The lack of fit test is not significant at α = `{python} g(lof_alpha)`.
4. Predictive power. Predicted R² falls short of R² by no more than `{python} f2(max_gap)`.
5. Residuals. Regressions of the absolute residuals on the predicted values, and of the residuals on run order, show no slope significant at α = `{python} g(lof_alpha)`, and no run has a Cook's distance above 4/n (`{python} f2(cook_lim)` for `{python} n_rsm` runs).

A model that fails criterion 3 or 4 was refitted with a justified change of terms, or it was not used to set a range. Where no adequate model resulted, the response is reported descriptively against its criterion over the runs of the design.

The PAR analysis follows PCMP-001 §6.4 and is described in @sec-par. Capability at commercial scale was estimated from the integrated model of the train, which runs `{python} mc_n` simulated batches with each parameter drawn within its NOR. Capability is reported as a one-sided Cpk against the drug substance criterion for each attribute of this step, and is judged against the target of `{python} f2(CPK_TARGET)` and the minimum of `{python} f2(CPK_MIN)` that PCMP-001 §7.9 sets, and the same simulation gives the probability of an out-of-specification drug substance.

# Study design

## Factors, ranges and the knowledge space

@tbl-params lists the parameters of the step with their set-point, NOR, range studied, study type and the classification proposed in @sec-class.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(rp)
print()
print(": Parameters of the Protein A step with set-point, NOR, range studied (Char. range), classification and study type. {#tbl-params}")
```

Load flow rate is set as a linear velocity, so at the set-point bed height it fixes the residence time. The residence time is `{python} g(rt_set)` min at the set-point flow rate, and over the range studied it runs from `{python} g(rt_hi)` min at the highest flow to `{python} g(rt_lo)` min at the lowest. The upper end of the flow range therefore tests the shortest residence time against the highest load, which is the condition most likely to cause breakthrough. The lower end of the elution pH range tests the strongest elution and the largest release of weakly bound host cell protein. The upper end tests the weakest elution, with the broadest peak and the least co-eluting host cell protein. @tbl-legend gives the letter code of each design factor, which the coefficient tables and the appendices use.

```{python}
print()
print(": Letter codes of the design factors. {#tbl-legend}")
```

The execution window of every study of the step is recorded in @tbl-chronology. Each study began after PCP-005 Version 1.0 was approved on `{python} plan_appr`.

## Screening design

The screening design (study S-PA-SCR, `{python} win('S-PA-SCR')`) was a full two-level factorial design in the `{python} n_fac` factors, with `{python} n_fact` factorial runs and `{python} cp_scr` centre points, `{python} n_scr` runs in all. Because the design is a full factorial, no effect is aliased with another, and every main effect and every two-factor interaction can be estimated. The responses were pool host cell protein, step yield and leached Protein A, with fragments by SEC recorded for information. All `{python} n_fac` factors were carried into the response-surface design whatever the screening result, as PCP-005 §6.2 planned. The screening design therefore served to identify effects and interactions and to check the ranges. Appendix A gives the matrix and the results.

## Response-surface design

The response-surface design (study S-PA-RSM, `{python} win('S-PA-RSM')`) was a face-centred central composite design in the same `{python} n_fac` factors. It has `{python} n_fact` factorial runs, `{python} n_axial` axial runs at the faces of the cube and `{python} cp_rsm` centre points, `{python} n_rsm` runs in all. A face-centred design keeps every run inside the range studied. The full quadratic model leaves `{python} int(F['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['model'].df_resid)` residual degrees of freedom, with `{python} F['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['df_pe']` for pure error and `{python} F['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['df_lof']` for lack of fit. The responses were pool host cell protein, step yield, leached Protein A and fragments by nrCE-SDS on the retained pools. Appendix B gives the matrix and the results.

## Univariate assessment

Operating temperature and bed height were studied one factor at a time in study S-PA-UNI (`{python} win('S-PA-UNI')`), with the other parameters at their set-points. Each was run `{python} uni_reps` times at the low and the high end of its range studied, and the `{python} uni_n_ref` set-point runs of study S-PA-SDM served as the reference, as PCP-005 §6.4 planned. Bed height was varied at the set-point linear velocity, so that the residence time changed with it. The shortest bed gives a residence time of `{python} g(rt_short)` min, shorter than any run of the designs. The responses were pool host cell protein, step yield and leached Protein A. Fragments were not measured in this study, which ran before AMD-001. A univariate study cannot detect an interaction. The ranges of these two parameters are therefore supported only with the other parameters at their set-points.

## Hold study of the Protein A eluate {#sec-holddesign}

The Protein A eluate is held at elution pH before viral inactivation. A pool produced at set-point was divided and held at `{python} t_cold` and `{python} t_warm` for up to `{python} h_days` days in study S-PA-HLD (`{python} win('S-PA-HLD')`). Samples were taken on days `{python} h_daylist` at each temperature. Aggregate and fragments were measured by SEC, and acidic variants by icIEF, at every sample point. The samples of days `{python} ' and '.join(str(int(x)) for x in ce_days)` were retained and tested by nrCE-SDS in study S-PA-RET. Because Protein A capture does not separate aggregate or charge variants, the held eluate carries the criteria that PCMP-001 sets for the output of the production bioreactor, ≤ `{python} agg_crit` % HMW and `{python} acid_crit` % acidic variants. Fragments are judged against the intermediate acceptance criterion of the pool, ≤ `{python} crit_frag` % by nrCE-SDS, on the days with an nrCE-SDS result.

Step yield was the most reproducible response, with a coefficient of variation of `{python} f2(cv_r.loc['Step yield', '%CV'])` % in the response-surface design. Pool host cell protein reproduced to `{python} f2(cv_r.loc[L['pool_hcp_ng_mg'], '%CV'])` % in the response-surface design and to `{python} f2(cv_s.loc[L['pool_hcp_ng_mg'], '%CV'])` % in the screening design. The larger screening value makes the screening tests for pool host cell protein less sensitive than those of the response-surface design. Leached Protein A was the least precise response, at `{python} f2(cv_r.loc[L['leached_protein_a_ppm'], '%CV'])` % in the response-surface design. Its centre-point spread is of the same size as its variation across the whole design, so the variation of the ELISA and of the runs at set-point masks any effect of the parameters of that size.

## Screening: factor effects

@tbl-scr-fit summarizes the screening models. The models for pool host cell protein and step yield are significant. The model for leached Protein A is not (`{python} pf(scr_fit.loc[L['leached_protein_a_ppm'], 'p-value'])`), and none of its terms is significant.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.fit_summary_df(UO, "screening"))
print()
print(": Screening model summary (main effects and two-factor interactions). {#tbl-scr-fit}")
```

Pool host cell protein was affected by elution buffer pH (B) and protein load (A), and by their interaction (AB). Raising the elution pH across its range lowered pool host cell protein by `{python} f0(abs(eH['B']['Effect']))` ng/mg, and raising protein load across its range raised it by `{python} f0(eH['A']['Effect'])` ng/mg. The AB interaction (`{python} f0(eH['AB']['Effect'])` ng/mg, `{python} pf(eH['AB']['p-value'])`) is negative, so the fall in host cell protein with rising pH is steeper at high load. Load flow rate and end of pool collect had no significant effect in the screening design. The effect of end of pool collect was positive in this design (`{python} f0(SV['D']['scr'])` ng/mg, `{python} pf(SV['D']['scr_p'])`), the opposite sign to the response-surface design (@sec-rsm). @tbl-scr-hcp gives the effects.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.screening_effects_df(UO, "pool_hcp_ng_mg"))
print()
print(": Screening effects on pool HCP (ng/mg), sorted by size. {#tbl-scr-hcp}")
```

Step yield was affected by end of pool collect (D), protein load (A) and load flow rate (C), and by the AC interaction. Extending the end of pool collect across its range raised yield by `{python} f"{100*eY['D']['Effect']:.1f}"` percentage points. Raising protein load and load flow rate lowered it by `{python} f"{100*abs(eY['A']['Effect']):.1f}"` and `{python} f"{100*abs(eY['C']['Effect']):.1f}"` percentage points. The AC interaction (`{python} f"{100*eY['AC']['Effect']:.1f}"` percentage points, `{python} pf(eY['AC']['p-value'])`) means that flow rate costs more yield at high load. The CD and BD interactions were also significant, at `{python} f"{100*eY['CD']['Effect']:.1f}"` and `{python} f"{100*eY['BD']['Effect']:.1f}"` percentage points. These are smaller than the main effects, and they were not confirmed in the response-surface design. Elution buffer pH had no significant effect on yield. @tbl-scr-yield gives the effects, and Appendix C gives the effects for leached Protein A.

```{python}

print()
print(": Screening effects on step yield (fraction), sorted by size. {#tbl-scr-yield}")
```

The screening results agree with the expectations of the platform history in direction for protein load and elution buffer pH and for the AB interaction on pool host cell protein, and for every main effect and the AC interaction on step yield. This type of design cannot attribute curvature to a factor, and the effects were refined in the response-surface design.

### Pool host cell protein

@tbl-coef-hcp gives the coefficients of the model for pool host cell protein, and @tbl-anova-hcp its analysis of variance.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.rsm_coeff_df(UO, "pool_hcp_ng_mg"))
print()
print(": Response-surface coefficients for pool HCP (ng/mg), coded units. {#tbl-coef-hcp}")
```

```{python}

show(_an.astype(object).where(_an.notna(), ""))
print()
print(": Analysis of variance with lack of fit for pool HCP (ng/mg). {#tbl-anova-hcp}")
```

The response-surface model confirms the screening result for protein load and elution buffer pH and refines it. Elution buffer pH (`{python} f0(cH['B']['Coef.'])` ng/mg per half range) and protein load (`{python} f0(cH['A']['Coef.'])` ng/mg) carry the largest coefficients, and the AB interaction is significant (`{python} f0(cH['AB']['Coef.'])` ng/mg, `{python} pf(cH['AB']['p-value'])`). At high load the pH coefficient is `{python} f0(slope_hi)` ng/mg per half range, and at low load it is `{python} f0(slope_lo)` ng/mg. The B² term is significant and positive (`{python} f0(cH['B²']['Coef.'])` ng/mg), so pool host cell protein rises more steeply at the low end of the pH range. The lack of fit test (`{python} pf(F['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['p_lof'])`) is close to its limit.

End of pool collect lowers pool host cell protein. Its coefficient is `{python} f0(cH['D']['Coef.'])` ng/mg per half range (`{python} pf(cH['D']['p-value'])`), an effect of `{python} f0(SV['D']['rsm'])` ng/mg across the range studied. The AD interaction (`{python} f0(cH['AD']['Coef.'])` ng/mg) makes the fall steeper at high load, and the BD interaction (`{python} f0(cH['BD']['Coef.'])` ng/mg) makes it shallower at high pH. Collecting further into the tail of the elution peak adds antibody with little host cell protein, because the weakly held impurity elutes early in the low-pH transition. The host cell protein per mass of antibody therefore falls, and it falls most where there is most impurity in the early part of the peak, at high load and low pH.

These three terms reverse sign between the designs. In the screening design the effect of end of pool collect was `{python} f0(SV['D']['scr'])` ng/mg, and the AD and BD effects were `{python} f0(SV['AD']['scr'])` and `{python} f0(SV['BD']['scr'])` ng/mg, against `{python} f0(SV['D']['rsm'])`, `{python} f0(SV['AD']['rsm'])` and `{python} f0(SV['BD']['rsm'])` ng/mg in the response-surface design. None of the screening estimates is significant, and each has a standard error of `{python} f0(scr_eff_se)` ng/mg. Noise alone does not explain the reversal, however. When the screening results are compared with the predictions of the response-surface model, the difference depends on end of pool collect by `{python} f0(disc_D)` ng/mg across its range (`{python} pf(disc_D_p)`). Curvature does not explain it either, because in a full factorial design the quadratic terms are confounded with the intercept and not with the main effect of end of pool collect. The cause was not identified (finding F10). The two designs were run at different times (@tbl-chronology), and a difference between their feeds or in how the end of collection was set could act in this way. The response-surface model is the predictive model, and the effect of end of pool collect is taken from it.

Load flow rate has no significant effect on pool host cell protein (`{python} pf(cH['C']['p-value'])`), and the AC interaction is not significant either (`{python} pf(cH['AC']['p-value'])`). Both point estimates are negative. The mechanism predicted a small rise in pool host cell protein with a faster load at high load, and the data do not support that prediction.

Across the response-surface design pool host cell protein ranged from `{python} f0(hcp_all_min)` to `{python} f0(hcp_all_max)` ng/mg. In `{python} n_hcp_over` runs of the two designs it exceeded the intermediate acceptance criterion of ≤ `{python} crit_hcp` ng/mg. `{python} 'Each of these runs was at the highest protein load and the lowest elution pH of the range studied, outside the NOR.' if hcp_over_corner else 'These runs lay at several settings of the design.'` @fig-contours shows the response surfaces over protein load and elution buffer pH, with load flow rate and end of pool collect at their set-points.

## Model residuals and influential runs {#sec-resid}

@tbl-resid gives the residual checks of criterion 5 of PCP-005 §7.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(res_df.to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
print()
print(": Residual checks of the response-surface models (PCP-005 §7, criterion 5). {#tbl-resid}")
```

No model shows a slope of the absolute residuals on the predicted values (the smallest p is `{python} f3(min(RES[r]['p_slope'] for r in RESP))`). `{python} 'No model shows a slope of the residuals on the run order of execution either' if order_ok else 'At least one model shows a slope of the residuals on the run order of execution'` (the smallest p is `{python} f3(p_order_min)`), so no drift over the course of the design is seen. Every model, however, has runs above the Cook's distance limit of 4/n, between `{python} n_over_min` and `{python} n_over_max` per response. Criterion 5 is therefore not met for any response. A full quadratic model of `{python} int(F['pool_hcp_ng_mg']['model'].df_model) + 1` terms in `{python} n_rsm` runs has a mean leverage of `{python} f2(mean_lev)`, and the factorial and axial runs of a face-centred design carry high leverage by construction. Cook's distances above 4/n are therefore expected in this design, and the limit does not separate an influential run from a run at a corner.

For pool host cell protein, which is the only model used to set a range, each run above the limit was deleted in turn and the model refitted. The coefficients of protein load and elution buffer pH changed by at most `{python} f"{loo_dmax:.0f}"` %. The highest prediction over the NOR moved between `{python} f0(loo_lo)` and `{python} f0(loo_hi)` ng/mg, and it `{python} "stayed below" if loo_ok else "did not stay below"` the criterion of `{python} crit_hcp` ng/mg in every case. No single run therefore decides the conclusion for pool host cell protein (finding F7). PCP-005 provides no alternative to the Cook's distance limit, so resting the conclusion on this influence analysis is a departure from the plan, and it is listed in @sec-dev.

## Mechanistic interpretation {#sec-mech}

Pool host cell protein rises as elution buffer pH falls, because a lower pH releases more of the host cell protein held weakly on the resin and on the antibody together with the product. A higher protein load puts more antibody on the bed, and with it more of the host cell protein associated with the antibody, so pool host cell protein rises with load. The negative AB interaction follows from the two effects acting on the same weakly bound impurity. At high load there is more of it on the bed, and a low elution pH releases more of it. The positive B² term shows that this release accelerates at the low end of the pH range.

End of pool collect lowers pool host cell protein per mass of antibody in the response-surface design. Collecting further into the tail adds antibody and little host cell protein, so the ratio falls. The same extension raises yield, which is the largest single effect on yield in both designs. The opposite sign of this effect in the screening design is not explained by the mechanism (finding F10).

A higher load flow rate shortens the residence time and lowers the dynamic binding capacity. This costs yield only when the bed is close to capacity, which is why the cost appears at high load and nearly vanishes at low load (the AC interaction). The mechanism also predicts a small rise in pool host cell protein at high load and high flow. The data show no such rise, and the point estimates point the other way.

Leached Protein A could not be modelled, and the mechanism gives no reason for it to follow the settings of a single run. The scale effect found in the qualification (@sec-sdm) is expected to have a different cause, the longer hold of the load before capture at manufacturing scale, which this study does not test. Fragments by nrCE-SDS fall slightly as elution pH rises, which is the direction expected from acid-catalysed hinge hydrolysis during elution. The effect is small because the antibody spends only the duration of the elution at low pH in the column.

For operation, elution buffer pH and protein load have the largest effects on pool host cell protein, and the risk lies in the corner of low pH and high load. End of pool collect is also associated with pool host cell protein, but within its NOR it does not move the boundary of that corner far (@sec-ds). Load flow rate is associated with lower yield at high load.

# Design space {#sec-ds}

The design space of this step is the region in protein load and elution buffer pH, the two WC-CPPs, over which pool host cell protein meets its intermediate acceptance criterion. Leached Protein A and fragments met their criteria in every run of the designs, and step yield has no criterion, so they do not constrain it. On the mean predictions of the response-surface model, with load flow rate and end of pool collect at their set-points, `{python} f"{ds2_sp:.0f}"` % of the plane of protein load and elution buffer pH over the range studied meets the criterion. With load flow rate and end of pool collect at the corners of their NORs, the fraction lies between `{python} f"{ds2_min:.0f}"` and `{python} f"{ds2_max:.0f}"` %. The excluded region is the corner of high protein load and low elution buffer pH shown in @fig-contours. At the boundary of a region defined on mean predictions, a single batch meets the criterion only about half the time [@amab2009], so the claim is made through the PARs of @sec-par, which use the 95 % prediction interval of a single run.

The ranges are nested. The NOR lies inside the characterized region, and the characterized region is the knowledge space within which a PAR can be claimed. Over the NOR the model predicts a mean pool host cell protein between `{python} cr_hcp_range` ng/mg (@tbl-criteria-protein-a). The upper limit of the 95 % prediction interval of a single run reaches at most `{python} f0(hcp_nor_pi_max)` ng/mg over the NOR, `{python} 'below' if hcp_nor_pi_max <= acc['pool_hcp_ng_mg'][1] else 'above'` the criterion. Movement outside the NOR and within a PAR would be assessed under change control. These statements rest on a model of the scale-down column, which is qualified for pool host cell protein (finding F1).

# Proven acceptable ranges {#sec-par}

## Acceptance basis

Each output of the step is judged against the intermediate acceptance criterion that PCMP-001 §7.3 derives a priori. The drug substance criterion is carried backward through the train using the worst case that each downstream step showed on the platform with X-Mab, Y-Mab and Z-Mab, and no margin is applied. For pool host cell protein the drug substance limit of ≤ `{python} ds_hcp` ng/mg is carried back through the platform worst cases of anion exchange and cation exchange, which together remove host cell protein `{python} fold_hcp`-fold. That gives ≤ `{python} crit_hcp` ng/mg. For leached Protein A the limit of ≤ `{python} ds_lpa` ppm is carried back through the same two steps, which together remove it `{python} fold_lpa`-fold, and gives ≤ `{python} crit_lpa` ppm. For fragments the limit of ≤ `{python} ds_frag` % is carried back through the lowest platform clearance of cation exchange, `{python} fold_frag`-fold, and the largest increase of low-pH viral inactivation, `{python} add_frag` percentage points. That gives ≤ `{python} crit_frag` %. The basis of each criterion is recorded as `{python} D.acceptance_basis(UO, 'pool_hcp_ng_mg')`. PCMP-001 Table 7.1 gives the derivation for the whole train.

These criteria rest on `{python} n_rel` platform worst cases of the downstream steps. `{python} 'Every one that could be checked against a response of the downstream designs was confirmed in PCR-006, PCR-007 and PCR-008.' if rel_all_conf else 'Not every one that could be checked against a downstream design was confirmed.'` The other `{python} n_rel - n_rel_chk` concern leached Protein A, which is not a response of the cation exchange or anion exchange designs, so the platform values stand. `{python} "No criterion of this step was tightened." if not any_tight else "At least one criterion of this step was tightened."` No criterion upstream of this step relies on a worst case of the Protein A step, so this report carries no verification of its own.

The decision statistic for a quality attribute is the 95 % prediction interval of a single run, because a single batch is what must meet a quality criterion (PCMP-001 §6.4). In the NOR-propagated analysis the model coefficients are drawn from their estimated covariance in every simulated run, together with the residual.
